question: A 55-year-old man comes to the physician because of fever, fatigue, dry cough, headache, and myalgia over the past week. Two days ago, he developed several painful oral lesions and difficulty swallowing. He underwent kidney transplantation 3 years ago. His temperature is 38.2°C (100.7°F). Physical examination shows bilateral rales, hepatosplenomegaly, and multiple 1–2 cm ulcerative lesions with raised borders in the oral mucosa. A photomicrograph of a liver biopsy specimen is shown. Which of the following is the most likely causal pathogen?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Kidney transplantation -> immunosuppression -> increased susceptibility to infections -> 85% CHAIN: Fever, fatigue, dry cough, headache, myalgia -> systemic symptoms -> possible systemic infection -> 70% CHAIN: Painful oral lesions, difficulty swallowing -> oral mucosa involvement -> oral infection -> 60% CHAIN: Liver biopsy showing specific pathogen -> likely causal pathogen identification -> 95% CHAIN: Multiple 1-2 cm ulcerative lesions with raised borders in oral mucosa -> characteristic of specific pathogen -> 90% CHAIN: Bilateral rales, hepatosplenomegaly -> systemic involvement -> disseminated infection -> 80% CHAIN: Photomicrograph of liver biopsy specimen showing specific morphology -> pathogen identification -> 100% CHAIN: Aspergillus fumigatus -> most likely causal pathogen -> 85%
analysis: The patient's history of kidney transplantation puts him at risk for opportunistic infections. The presence of oral lesions and difficulty swallowing suggests an oral infection. The photomicrograph of the liver biopsy specimen is likely to show characteristic findings of the causal pathogen. Given the clinical presentation and the immunocompromised state post kidney transplantation, the most likely causal pathogen is Candida albicans, a common opportunistic fungal infection in transplant recipients.
